content: 1. In two trials, there was an unclear risk of bias related to allocation concealment, and in one trial, there was an unclear risk of bias in selective reporting. Additionally, one trial demonstrated a high risk of bias in the blinding of outcome assessment and incomplete outcome data. 2. Breastfeeding counseling should be provided as a standard of care to pregnant women and mothers who are considering or already breastfeeding. This intervention aims to improve breastfeeding practices. The preferences and values of mothers, as well as the acceptability of breastfeeding counseling among stakeholders, are critical factors that influence the outcomes. 3. Many women reported receiving inadequate education and advice about infant feeding during pregnancy. The issue was more about insufficient time allocated per session rather than poor quality of counseling. 4. Women appreciated antenatal counseling and the opportunity to meet a health worker or counselor before delivery. Missing this opportunity was often seen as a significant gap in care. 5. Women emphasized the importance of follow-up sessions to address challenges and celebrate successes in breastfeeding. This was consistent across studies conducted in both highand low-income countries. 6. In the context of HIV testing, women expressed discomfort with being counseled about feeding options immediately after learning their HIV status. They preferred more time to process the information. 7. Women living with HIV desired more frequent counseling and follow-up sessions rather than receiving a large amount of information in a single session. Counselors agreed but noted concerns that women might not return for follow-up visits, leading them to condense all information into one session. 8. Adolescent mothers often lacked routine, continued contact with health professionals after the early postnatal period. Many believed that all benefits of counseling were gained in the initial days after delivery. 9. Mothers of low socioeconomic status in high-income countries reported limited positive interactions with medical professionals during the postpartum period. They often cited a lack of contact with medical staff compared to interactions with peer counselors, which were perceived as more helpful. 10. Nurses highlighted the need for more time to spend with women, both in hospitals and during home visits. They also emphasized the importance of individualized follow-up support rather than adhering to rigid schedules. 11. Health-care professionals described hospital environments as busy and hectic, which limited the time available for breastfeeding support. Mothers and midwives also noted this lack of time as a barrier to effective breastfeeding counseling. 12. Nurses in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) faced challenges in helping mothers maintain their milk supply. They recognized the need for follow-up support, especially since infants are often discharged only when they can feed without assistance, which may encourage bottle feeding. 13. Women wanted autonomy and respect for their choices during breastfeeding counseling. They appreciated when their preferences were acknowledged and supported. 14. Current antenatal classes were often seen as insufficiently inclusive of fathers and partners. Both mothers and staff highlighted this gap in care. 15. Women particularly valued home-based care when sufficient time was allowed for breastfeeding to occur in a relaxed environment. 16. Mothers living with HIV and their counselors often had differing perspectives on the effectiveness and structure of counseling sessions. 17. Midwives emphasized the importance of observing breastfeeding sessions to provide individualized support tailored to each mother’s needs. 18. Medical staff acknowledged that women living with HIV often received conflicting messages from different clinics and staff members. Both health-care professionals and mothers described challenges related to inconsistent information. 19. Health workers encouraged mothers to rely on embodied knowledge or other indicators to assess whether their baby was receiving enough milk, as direct observation of milk intake is not possible. 20. Some midwives were aware of the personal nature of breastfeeding and recognized that mothers might be sensitive to how their breasts were touched during counseling. 21. Nurses and lactation consultants suggested that antenatal breast examinations could be helpful to assess breast and nipple shape and address potential issues, such as flat nipples, before delivery. 22. Women desired continuity of care, as having multiple counselors often led to insecurity and uncertainty, particularly when conflicting advice was given.
